executive_summary: Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania and the Netherlands agreed to jointly purchase more than 430 CV90 infantry fighting vehicles from BAE Systems Hagglunds, an outlay estimated to exceed 7.5 billion euros, with the contract entering force only once all five sign simultaneously at a ceremony scheduled this Friday in Stockholm; separately the UK Ministry of Defence awarded Babcock an £8 billion Gateway Agreement, which Babcock said is worth £8.7 billion over five years and is effective from 1 December. The read is that European land and naval industrial capacity is being locked into multi-year framework commitments faster than budgets are debated, and I would be proven wrong if the Stockholm signature slips or a participant follows Estonia, which signed a 2025 declaration of intent and subsequently withdrew. Watch the simultaneous five-nation CV90 signing in Stockholm this Friday: completion confirms the 7.5 billion euro programme and BAE Systems Hagglunds order flow, while a missing signature would reopen the question of how durable joint procurement is.
opportunity_of_the_day: Firefly Aerospace closed Wednesday at $18.14, down 19 percent year to date, as Needham initiated Buy with a $35 target on November 25 against record backlog of $1.7 billion and Q3 revenue up 259.6 percent to $110.68 million; the read is that the gap is worth taking only if launch cadence converts backlog.
risk_of_the_day: China suspension of its antimony export ban to the US expires on November 27, 2026, with China, Russia and Tajikistan controlling about 90 percent of a market producing 110,000 metric tons in 2025; the implication is that defence and energy buyers face input repricing within days of expiry, not quarters.

space.signal: China suspension of its antimony export ban to the US is set to expire on November 27, 2026, with China accounting for 40,000 of the 110,000 metric tons produced in 2025, or roughly 36.37 percent.
space.watch: Antimony export ban suspension expiry, November 27
space.bull: Continued supply access keeps a US Geological Survey critical mineral available to defence and photovoltaic buyers without the cost shock that reprices hardware backlogs.
space.bear: A reinstated ban removes roughly 36.37 percent of global output from US-bound supply and pushes qualification and inventory costs onto every defence and energy manufacturer exposed to it.

defence.signal: The five-nation CV90 contract for more than 430 vehicles, estimated to exceed 7.5 billion euros, enters into force only once Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania and the Netherlands sign a joint order simultaneously at a ceremony scheduled this Friday in Stockholm.
defence.watch: Stockholm simultaneous five-nation CV90 joint order signing
defence.bull: Completion converts a multi-nation declaration into a live programme, with Finland alone detailing 160 vehicles plus an option on 100 more at 2.8 billion euros, and validates pooled European land procurement.
defence.bear: A delayed or partial signature, after Estonia withdrew from the initiative following its 2025 declaration of intent, would show that joint buys remain reversible and that order books built on them are not yet firm.

geo.signal: The Libyan National Army has vowed to retaliate at the appropriate time and place after Ukrainian sea drones hit the Russian corvette Merkury in the civilian part of Benghazi port and two LNA officers died of their wounds on November 24, with no date given for any response.
geo.watch: LNA retaliation vow after Benghazi corvette strike
geo.bull: If no retaliation materialises and the Turkey-Libya maritime deal published on November 25 in the Libyan official gazette holds, eastern Mediterranean exploration and shipping risk premia stay contained.
geo.bear: Retaliation around Benghazi port, already shown to be a Russian refuelling and resupply point, would extend the Ukraine war into North African energy and port infrastructure and raise insurance and logistics costs across the basin.

stocks.notable_movers: At its last close ASTS led the tracked names, gaining more than 10 percent to $26.02, signalling continued speculative appetite for low-earth-orbit connectivity plays despite the broader conflict risk picture; RKLB added 2.26 percent to $47.02 while LMT rose 2.15 percent to $599.24, with defence primes broadly modestly higher at the last close, consistent with elevated procurement signals across this edition. OUTLOOK: Counter-drone and uncrewed systems suppliers face the most immediate demand tailwind as NATO members, France, and the Pentagon all accelerate procurement simultaneously, though investors should watch whether Libya instability tightens Strait of Hormuz risk further and pressures energy-dependent European defence budgets before year end.
stocks.sector_outlook: Counter-drone and uncrewed systems suppliers face the most immediate demand tailwind as NATO members, France, and the Pentagon all accelerate procurement simultaneously, though investors should watch whether Libya instability tightens Strait of Hormuz risk further and pressures energy-dependent European defence budgets before year end.

stories.headline: Starship Flight 15 booster splashes in Gulf
stories.context: SpaceX attempted a double-catch of Starship hardware during Flight 15 but aborted the initial catch mid-test, sending the booster into the Gulf of Mexico rather than returning it to the launch tower. The failure underscores the engineering precision required to scale chopstick-arm recovery to Starship dimensions, where millisecond timing and wind shifts can defeat the manoeuvre. Major commercial satellite operators, defence contractors and NASA rely on Starship eventually hitting heavy-payload cost targets to make deep-space logistics commercially viable.
stories.implication: Until SpaceX demonstrates consistent booster recovery at Starship scale, the full reusability cost model underpinning its commercial and government launch pricing remains unvalidated, exposing customers and investors to schedule and cost uncertainty.

stories.headline: SpaceX to donate shares to Trump Account holders
stories.context: SpaceX announced it will donate one newly issued Class A common share to every currently active Trump Account, the tax-advantaged investment vehicle created for eligible children in the United States, while CEO Elon Musk pledged to personally match the contribution from his own holdings. The corporate portion involves newly issued shares, while Musk contribution comes from his personal stake. SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell and her husband separately committed more than two million SpaceX shares to children Trump Accounts, confirmed in the November 25 statement.
stories.implication: The initiative broadens SpaceXs retail ownership base and creates long-term reputational alignment with a government policy vehicle, but the new share issuance introduces dilution risk for current holders at a moment when SpaceXs operational credibility is being tested by the Flight 15 booster failure.

stories.headline: China antimony export ban suspension expires Nov 27
stories.context: China suspension of its antimony export ban to the US is set to expire on November 27, 2026, returning supply security to the foreground for defence and energy sector buyers. Global antimony production in 2025 averaged 110,000 metric tons, with China accounting for 40,000 metric tons, or roughly 36.37 percent, while China along with Russia and Tajikistan controls about 90 percent of global antimony production. Antimony is classified as a critical mineral by the US Geological Survey, with flame retardants accounting for roughly 50 percent of global use and the photovoltaic sector identified as a key long-term demand driver.
stories.implication: Expiry of the suspension tightens the near-term supply chain for defence-relevant antimony applications including lead-acid batteries and flame retardants, increasing the investment case for domestic US antimony exploration and production assets.

stories.headline: Firefly stock falls as Needham sets $35 target
stories.context: Firefly Aerospace shares were down to $18.14 as of Wednesday close, bringing the year-to-date decline to 19 percent, even as Needham initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $35 price target on November 25. Needham described Firefly as a rapidly maturing space ecosystem company well positioned to fill large supply gaps in the launch market, citing proven small- and medium-lift launch capability and lunar lander experience. Firefly quarter-end backlog reached a record $1.7 billion, and Q3 revenue rose 259.6 percent year over year to $110.68 million.
stories.implication: The divergence between a bullish analyst initiation and continued share price erosion signals that market participants are pricing execution risk and near-term revenue visibility ahead of long-term addressable market arguments, a dynamic operators and launch customers should factor into Fireflys schedule reliability assumptions.

stories.headline: Ukraine drones strike Russian corvette in Benghazi
stories.context: Ukrainian sea drones hit the Russian corvette Merkury in the civilian part of Benghazi port, where it had docked to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and Khalifa Haftar eastern government, with the drones most likely launched from Misrata. Two officers of Haftar Libyan National Army died of their wounds on November 24, and the LNA has vowed to retaliate at the appropriate time and place. Haftar flew to Turkey the same day on his first known visit, and on November 25 his parliament published the Turkey-Libya maritime deal in Libya official gazette, opening waters off the eastern coast to Turkish exploration.
stories.implication: The strike extends Ukraines uncrewed maritime reach into the Mediterranean, threatens the fragile Libyan political settlement underpinning a $20 billion oil investment pitch, and positions Turkey as an immediate beneficiary of the resulting power vacuum, all of which elevate insurance and operational risk for energy infrastructure operators across the eastern Mediterranean.

stories.headline: Houthi strike kills worker at Saudi Jazan refinery
stories.context: A Houthi strike on a refinery in Jazan, southern Saudi Arabia, killed a Nepali worker and injured several others of different nationalities, triggering a temporary shutdown of some operations and sparking a fire, according to the Saudi Press Agency citing the energy ministry. The Saudi-led military coalition said it destroyed the Houthi missile launch platform in Yemen Hodeidah used in the attack on the refinery. Saudi forces also intercepted two ballistic missiles launched towards Riyadh, a cruise missile in western Saudi Arabia and a drone near Jeddah port, with no civilian injuries reported from falling debris; Iran denied responsibility for a separate drone attack on a Kuwaiti air-defence site that killed two Italian technicians from Rheinmetall Italia.
stories.implication: Simultaneous attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and a NATO-allied nations technicians inside Kuwait raise the operational risk threshold for all foreign defence contractors and energy sector workers across the Gulf, with direct consequences for insurance underwriting and site security procurement.

stories.headline: UK awards Babcock £8B submarine maintenance deal
stories.context: The UK Ministry of Defence awarded Babcock an £8 billion Gateway Agreement to transform submarine maintenance and delivery of critical naval base services, targeting faster return-to-sea times for Royal Navy submarines and directly strengthening the nuclear deterrent. The contract will create around 3,000 highly skilled roles including 900 jobs and 450 apprentice and graduate opportunities at His Majesty Naval Base Clyde, and is described as the second major multi-billion submarine-related deal signed since the defence investment plan. Babcock said the agreement, effective from 1 December, is the largest contract in its history and is worth £8.7 billion over five years.
stories.implication: The £8 billion award to Babcock consolidates its position as the primary UK submarine sustainment prime and signals that the Ministry of Defence is prioritising deterrent readiness over procurement diversification, reducing near-term competitive opportunity for rival maintainers but creating a stable long-horizon revenue base for Babcock and its supply chain at Clyde.

stories.headline: Five NATO nations jointly buy 430+ CV90 vehicles
stories.context: Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania and the Netherlands agreed to jointly purchase more than 430 CV90 infantry fighting vehicles manufactured by BAE Systems Hagglunds in what Finnish Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen described as the largest joint land defence purchase in NATO, with an outlay estimated to exceed 7.5 billion euros. The contract enters into force once all five nations sign a joint order simultaneously at a ceremony scheduled this Friday in Stockholm, with Finland already detailing its portion as 160 vehicles, with an option to acquire 100 more, for a value of 2.8 billion euros. Estonia signed a 2025 declaration of intent but subsequently withdrew from the initiative.
stories.implication: A confirmed signing this Friday would lock in the largest pooled NATO land procurement on record, validating the Nordic Defence Cooperation model and signalling that European allies are prepared to execute large platform commitments without waiting for the EU budget impasse to resolve.

stories.headline: Pentagon delivers 25,000+ drone systems to CENTCOM
stories.context: The US Department of War announced that more than 25,000 drone and counter-drone systems were delivered to US Central Command by the Pentagon Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems, with more than 24,000 counter-unmanned aerial systems delivered specifically through Joint Interagency Task Force 401, described as capable of creating a multi-layered defensive shield. The announcement followed the September announcement of the Autonomous Warfare Command and cited Under Secretary Hegseth direction as the driving authority for fielding at the speed of modern combat. The Pentagon said it will expand fielding pipelines for the technology to Pacific Command, European Command and the broader military force.
stories.implication: The scale of this delivery underlines that counter-UAS is now a volume procurement problem rather than a niche capability gap, favouring suppliers with established production throughput and logistics integration over emerging technology entrants without manufacturing scale.

stories.headline: Russia hybrid sabotage on Europe rose in past year
stories.context: The International Institute for Strategic Studies reported that sabotage attacks on European infrastructure rose by 16 percent in the 12 months leading up to September 2026, with arson and use of explosives roughly doubling over that period. Targeting of critical infrastructure including military-industrial and transport sites accounted for more than half of recorded incidents between October 2025 and September 2026, while a semi-skilled tier of operatives is now using more complex methods including improvised explosive devices with timed and remote detonators alongside unskilled recruits who carry out most operations. The IISS assessed that the campaign has failed in its objective of deterring European support for Ukraine, with military assistance to Ukraine from Western allies continuing to increase.
stories.implication: The 16 percent rise and shift toward more sophisticated methods signals that European defence manufacturers, logistics nodes and transport infrastructure face a structurally elevated threat environment that will sustain procurement demand for physical security, detection and resilience capabilities well beyond the duration of active hostilities.

stories.headline: Iran denies Kuwait drone strike that killed two Italians
stories.context: Two Italian technicians — Antonio Saccoccio and Emanuele Lo Russo — were killed when drones struck a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, with Kuwait and Italy both blaming Iran. Iran armed forces spokesperson denied any role, calling it a false-flag operation, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation. The two men were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system and were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports.
stories.implication: The first European civilian deaths in the US-Israel-Iran confrontation raise the stakes for NATO-aligned defence contractors operating across Gulf states, where air defence integration work now carries direct lethal risk.

stories.headline: Lebanon judiciary pursues Hezbollah in explosives cases
stories.context: Lebanese military judges issued search notices for three Hezbollah officials including Bilal al-Asaad, and in-person arrest warrants for five suspects detained in northern Lebanon, following charges of forming an armed group and recruiting and arming its members. The proceedings follow the Lebanese government March 2 decision banning Hezbollah military and security activities, though defence lawyers denied the suspects had conducted a security reconnaissance mission and the charges have yet to be proven. Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem demanded the release of those detained and defended the legality of the activities of those held in the Dahr al-Baidar case.
stories.implication: The Lebanese states willingness to prosecute Hezbollah members through military courts represents a structural shift in internal security dynamics, with implications for stability and foreign investment risk in Lebanon.

stories.headline: DARPA and Ukraine race to field battlefield rescue drones
stories.context: Ukrainian innovators are pioneering frontline aerial drone evacuation of casualties, while DARPA is developing AI-assisted robots designed to find and assess injured troops and civilians on the battlefield, according to Defense News. The competing approaches reflect a broader race to integrate autonomous systems into casualty recovery, one of the time-critical and dangerous tasks in modern combat.
stories.implication: Parallel US government and Ukrainian investment in AI-driven casualty recovery systems signals a new procurement category for autonomous medical and search robotics that defence technology investors should track alongside offensive drone programmes.

stories.headline: QBE Asia: supplier concentration deepens cyber risk
stories.context: QBE Asia published a report finding that Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud accounted for 63 percent of enterprise cloud network spending in 2025, creating systemic risk where disruption at a single provider spreads across multiple companies and sectors. The report quantified downtime costs at an average of USD $15,000 per minute, with ransomware causing affected organisations an average of 24 days of direct operational downtime, and 60 percent of small companies targeted in cyber attacks forced to shut down operations within six months of an incident. The report also found that the industrialisation of artificial intelligence has cut the time between initial access and exploitation to 30 minutes, down from about 100 minutes in 2021.
stories.implication: Extreme cloud concentration among three providers represents a single-point-of-failure risk for defence supply chains and space operators that rely on commercial cloud infrastructure, making provider diversification and sovereign cloud capability a growing strategic imperative.

stories.headline: Italy claims 2.8% of GDP in defence spend for 2026
stories.context: Italian officials told Defense News that Rome reached a combined defence and domestic security spend equal to 2.8 percent of GDP in 2026, fulfilling a commitment made at the July NATO summit, with core defence spending calculated at 2.1 percent and domestic security at 0.7 percent. Pure defence spending, labelled Funzione Difesa, was extrapolated from budget figures at 23.6 billion euros, up from 22.49 billion euros the year before, though the official budget document does not clearly state the totals. The NATO budget total is listed at 48.31 billion euros, equal to 2.1 percent of GDP, up from 2 percent in 2025.
stories.implication: Italys claimed achievement of the 2.8 percent threshold, if accepted by NATO, sets a precedent for how allies may structure and present blended security budgets to meet alliance targets under US pressure to reach 5 percent by 2035.

stories.headline: France launches counter-drone industry pact to 2027
stories.context: France kicked off a new counter-drone pact with its defence industry, running to the end of summer 2027 and extending an existing drone pact to cover counter-drone capabilities, bringing together firms and military end users under the leadership of the Directorate General for Armament and industry association Gicat. France junior minister for the armed forces said the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East had been a quite brutal reality check and that French forces have an urgent need for counter-drone capabilities, adding that France has already faced problems related to having insufficient counter-drone capability. The new pact covers systems to counter unmanned aerial vehicles but also maritime and ground drones, and Gicat chairman Emmanuel Levacher said he expects most or all of the 200 partners in the drone pact to participate.
stories.implication: The structured pact model, cutting procurement red tape and focusing on fast contract delivery, is becoming a replicable template across European militaries seeking to close counter-drone gaps without full programme timelines.
